confidence_note: Well-documented core of Lansing's narrative. The reference TR text has errors that must not be carried over: the James Caird carried six men (Shackleton plus five), not five; the crossing took about 16 days, not 17; the distance is roughly 800 nautical miles, not 1,300 km; 22 men (not 'the whole crew') waited on Elephant Island; the rescue took four attempts. Omitted: exact sight counts, day-by-day details of the boat journey, direct quotes. Added later: ice chipping, screws in boots and rope, three failed rescue attempts, all recalled from Lansing and the general record (medium-high); kept to one clause each.
facts: Shackleton's ship Endurance was trapped in the Weddell Sea pack ice in 1915, drifted with it for months, and was crushed and sank in November 1915; the 28-man crew made camp on the ice.
When the ice broke up the men took to three lifeboats and reached Elephant Island in April 1916.
Elephant Island was uninhabited and far from shipping lanes; nobody knew where the expedition was, so no rescue would come by itself.
Shackleton chose the strongest boat, the James Caird (about 22.5 ft / 6.9 m); the carpenter, Harry McNish, built it up with a deck from sledge runners, box lids and canvas.
Six men sailed: Shackleton, Frank Worsley, Tom Crean, McNish, Timothy McCarthy and John Vincent. Twenty-two stayed behind under Frank Wild.
The target was South Georgia, about 800 nautical miles away across the Southern Ocean; Worsley navigated with a sextant and only a handful of sun sightings through cloud.
The crossing took about 16 days; they landed on the wrong (uninhabited) side of South Georgia.
Shackleton, Worsley and Crean then crossed South Georgia's unmapped mountainous interior on foot in about 36 hours to reach the Stromness whaling station.
The men on Elephant Island were rescued on 30 August 1916 on the fourth rescue attempt; every one of the 28 survived.
Ice kept forming on the James Caird and the men had to chip it off so it would not capsize her.
For the South Georgia crossing, screws were driven into their boots for grip and they carried rope; the first three rescue attempts to Elephant Island were turned back by ice.
scene_details: A 6.9 m open boat decked with sledge runners, box lids and canvas.
Worsley taking sun sights with a sextant when the clouds opened.
Twenty-two men waiting on a rocky island nobody knew they were on.
tension: Waiting meant certain silence; leaving meant an open boat across the Southern Ocean with 22 men depending on a navigator who could rarely see the sun.
opening_idea: Open on Worsley, the sextant and the rare gaps in the cloud, with 22 men staking their lives on those few readings.

lessons.idea: Waiting is also a risky choice; count its cost next to the cost of acting.
lessons.anchor: Nobody knew where they were on Elephant Island, so waiting meant no rescue

reflect_final: In what situation where you are waiting for an answer would you set a date to stop waiting and start the next step, and what date would you pick?

use_cases.situation: A supplier has gone silent and the team keeps saying 'let's wait a bit'.
use_cases.move: Say that waiting has a cost too, and propose a Friday deadline after which a second option opens.

use_cases.situation: A friend has waited for a reply on a job for weeks.
use_cases.move: Ask what date they would stop waiting and what second door they would try.

use_cases.situation: You are postponing a decision that nobody else will make for you.
use_cases.move: Write down what waiting costs each week and set the date you will act, as Shackleton did when no rescue could come.

pocket_idea: On Elephant Island nobody was coming, so waiting was a decision too: price the wait and set an end date.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: Twenty-two men waited on an island nobody knew about while six sailed 800 miles guided by a few glimpses of the sun.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Endurance crushed, 28 men on Elephant Island, six in the James Caird, 800 miles, 16 days, mountains, rescue on fourth try, all alive.
